item.title: Google Begins Rolling Out Personal AI Assistant, Tasks, In India
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Big tech giant Google has begun rolling out its new agentic AI assistant Tasks, formerly Gemini Sparks, to users in…
item.content:encoded:
Big tech giant Google has begun rolling out its new agentic AI assistant Tasks, formerly Gemini Sparks, to users in India. 

In a blogpost, Josh Woodward, the vice-president of Google Labs and the Gemini app, said that the new feature will enable users to assign tasks to the AI assistant, including making calls, booking appointments, comparing products and completing purchases.

The service comes bundled for free with Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. 

“Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model,” said Woodward.

It is pertinent to note that Tasks was reportedly initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, an agentic AI helper. It was subsequently expanded to the US-based subscribers of the Google AI Ultra tier. Google is now rolling out this feature for free in six markets.

Unlike Gemini’s Chat that only generates responses to a user’s queries, Tasks goes one step further and enables the chatbot to perform basic functions. With the rollout, Google could be looking to expand the role of AI assistants beyond answering questions to embedding them in daily life. 

In his blog post, Woodward noted that Gemini can draw on information already available within Google services, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, files and payment cards, to carry out tasks on a user’s behalf. With Tasks, he also said that Gemini can call businesses, wait through hold periods, identify available appointment slots and add bookings to a user’s calendar. 

Under the hood, Gemini uses the agent payments protocol (AP2) to enable Tasks to make purchases online. Going forward, the big tech giant said that it plans to integrate the universal commerce protocol (UCP) into Gemini to further streamline the checkout experience. 

Google also said that it is working with American Express, Mastercard and Visa to enable  tokenised card transactions via Tasks. However, the big tech juggernaut did not specify whether partnerships extend to India too. 

That said, India’s inclusion in the initial rollout gives Google a large market to test consumer adoption of the personal AI assistant feature. To further scale the rollout, Google has also invited app developers to join its Connected Apps Platform, which could pave the way for Indian consumer, fintech, travel tech and foodtech brands to build task-based third-party integrations with the assistant.

These features could make Gemini Tasks a channel for online shopping, bill payments and routine purchases. However, adoption will depend on the availability of supported merchants, payment methods and third-party apps in the country. There appears to be no clarity on this front.

The launch is part of a broader wave of big tech giants rolling out personal AI assistants to capture the masses. In September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg showcased the company’s new offering called Muse, which allows an AI agent to send emails, fill forms, make plans and even make purchases autonomously. 

Prior to this, OpenAI also introduced Dots that can draft board meeting decks, conduct background research, and handle multi-step project management. xAI has also been developing Grok Bot, which sees cleaning up sales records and processing invoices as potential uses for agents.

Microsoft is also pursuing agents, built on OpenClaw, which can function as digital teammates. Back home, Emergent, better known for its vibe-coding platform, launched Wingman, an autonomous agent that handles routine actions and seeks approval before taking bigger steps.

item.title: Amazon To Invest $7 Bn In Indian Green Energy Projects By 2030
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Ecommerce giant Amazon has announced plans to invest $7 Bn in renewable energy projects across India by 2030. The company…
item.content:encoded:
Ecommerce giant Amazon has announced plans to invest $7 Bn in renewable energy projects across India by 2030. The company said that the latest commitment will be in addition to the $4 Bn that it has deployed in renewable energy investments in the country.

In a statement, Amazon said that the latest investment will go towards “significantly” expanding its renewable energy portfolio in India. 

“… This additional investment of $7 Bn underlines our long-term commitment, helping bring additional wind and solar capacity online while contributing to India’s energy security and long-term renewable energy ambitions,” said Amazon’s chief sustainability officer Kara Hurst.

Hurst further added that Amazon’s investment will look to expand access to renewable energy at scale in the country and contribute to India’s goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2070.

In a statement, the company also announced four new wind and solar projects with a combined total capacity of 934 megawatts (MWs). This includes a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka and another 200 MW combined solar-and-wind farm in the state. The new projects also include a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh and another 200 MW solar one in Rajasthan.

Part of Amazon’s existing $4 Bn in contracted projects in the country, the company said that these projects were secured through power purchase agreements and long-term contracts. Under this, the ecommerce major will be able to buy electricity from the operators of these projects. 

With these renewable energy investments in India, Amazon plans to reduce the carbon intensity of the electricity powering its operations by 65% by 2030.

Overall, Amazon claims that its renewable energy portfolio in India includes 14 “utility-scale” wind and solar projects as well as 43 on-site solar installations across its facilities in the country. 

The ecommerce giant also claims to have so far deployed more than 15,000 electric vehicles across more than 500 Indian cities. It also reiterated that it is partnering with Tata Motors to deploy 3,000 electric trucks in the country. 

The commitment comes as Amazon continues to double down on India. In September, reports surfaced that the ecommerce giant was planning to invest $3 Bn (₹28,790 Cr) to expand its quick commerce business, Amazon Now, in India over the course of next four years. 

Last year, Amazon India had announced a ₹2,000 Cr investment to add 17 new fulfilment centres, six sortation centres, and 75 last-mile delivery stations across India. Prior to this, it had also committed an investment of $35 Bn across its India businesses till 2030 to help boost its cumulative exports from the country to $80 Bn by 2030

item.title: Airtel Payments Bank’s Profit Zooms 139% YoY To ₹28 Cr In Q2
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Airtel Payments Bank’s net profit zoomed 139% to ₹28.2 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27…
item.content:encoded:
Airtel Payments Bank’s net profit zoomed 139% to ₹28.2 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) compared to ₹11.8 Cr in the year-ago quarter. 

The company attributed the surge in the bottom line to rising revenues, improving margins and growing adoption of its services. 

In a statement, Airtel Payments Bank also said that its revenues grew 8.9% to ₹875.5 Cr in the quarter under review as against ₹804 Cr in Q2 FY26. Meanwhile, EBITDA zoomed 39.4% YoY to ₹124.5 Cr in the quarter under review.

The payments bank also said that it crossed ₹3,500 Cr in annualised revenue in Q2 FY27, with annualised net profit hovering around the ₹113 Cr mark. The company also claimed that it is currently clocking an annualised EBITDA of ₹500 Cr.

“… Our sustained growth and profitability reflect the maturity of our business model. We continue to see solid uptake of our offerings across consumers and merchants, serving seamlessly across the value chain of payments. As digital adoption deepens across the country, we remain focused on driving customer engagement, deepening our offerings and strengthening our leadership in digital banking,” said Airtel Payments Bank MD and CEO Anubrata Biswas.

On the operational front, the payments bank said that monthly transacting users (for savings bank account) grew 21.1% YoY to 3.1 Cr during the quarter under review, while customer balances grew 10% YoY to nearly ₹4,385 Cr.

The company also noted that it operated a merchant network of over 5 Lakh at the end of September 2026. On the B2B front, the payments bank said that it digitises around ₹7,000 Cr worth of cash every month for businesses via its cash management and collection services. 

Airtel Payments Bank also said that it has so far issued 70 Lakh National Common Mobility Cards (NCMC), adding that it processes three out of every four transit payments in the country. It also claims to process half of India’s remittances and 25% of total AePS (Aadhaar Enabled Payment System) transactions.

Airtel Payments Bank commenced operations in early 2017 with a seed investment of $440 Mn. It was the only profitable payments bank in the country in Q2 FY27 as rival Fino Payments Bank slipped into the red during the quarter. 

Airtel Payments Bank offers digital banking solutions as well as insurance, lending, soundbox and investment services to customers across both urban and rural India. 

The results come a couple of months after Sunil Bharti Mittal stepped down as the non-executive chairman of Airtel Payments Bank (and also left the company’s board) after more than a decade. Following his departure, existing board member Shabnam Sinha took over as chairperson on October 1 for a period of three years.

item.title: Coinbase India Partially Resumes INR Withdrawals After A Week Of Disruption
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Following a week of disruption, cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase has partially resumed processing INR withdrawals for users in India.  In a…
item.content:encoded:
Following a week of disruption, cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase has partially resumed processing INR withdrawals for users in India. 

In a post on social media platform X, the platform said that the outage at one of its banking partners disrupted payouts for all of its clients. Coinbase India further noted that it has now begun processing all failed INR withdrawals, pending since November 9, in batches through an alternative banking route. 

The crypto exchange noted that the first batch has been processed, adding that the remaining batches will follow soon. 

However, the platform is yet to fully resume withdrawals. Coinbase India said that the INR withdrawal option on its app will still remain unavailable, citing outage issues at its banking partner. The company has directed users to contact its support team for withdrawals in the interim.

“In light of this banking failure, we are strengthening our banking setup in India and will share more on this soon,” said Coinbase India.

The exchange also assured users that their funds remain safe. It also said that customers will receive push notifications and email confirmations once their withdrawals have been initiated.

This comes a week after Coinbase India, on November 9, said that it was temporarily suspending INR withdrawals due to an outage at its banking partner. The move had prompted public outcry from its customers online, with many seeking more clarity on the timeline for disbursals. 

The development comes barely five months after the crypto exchange relaunched its platform in India after a two year-long hiatus. The platform had exited India in 2023 after Indian authorities tightened its scrutiny around the unregulated asset class. 

Subsequently, it secured the requisite licensing to operate as a cryptocurrency exchange from the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) in March last year, paving the way for its return to one of the top cryptocurrency markets globally.

It is important to mention that Coinbase is one of the largest cryptocurrency exchanges globally, and is also listed on the Nasdaq.

At the heart of all this is the Indian cryptocurrency market, which is projected to become a $14 Bn opportunity by 2034. However, Indian authorities continue to be wary of the crypto ecosystem. 

Just last year, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra said that cryptos may affect the country’s financial stability. On top of this, a Parliamentary standing committee on finance recently termed the asset class as “high risk” citing rampant money laundering, trafficking, radicalisation and suspicious crypto transactions.

item.title: Apple Pay & iCloud Report Outages, Company Blames Internal Update
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: A widespread outage at iPhone maker Apple has brought many of its services to a standstill for thousands of users…
item.content:encoded:
A widespread outage at iPhone maker Apple has brought many of its services to a standstill for thousands of users globally. 

According to DownDetector, users began to experience issues with some of Apple’s services at 9:51 PM IST on November 17. As per the outage tracking website, many of the big tech giant’s online services were reporting issues, including Apple Pay, iCloud, App Store, Apple Business Manager, Apple Music and Apple Support.

Confirming the development, Apple’s systems update page noted that iCloud Mail, ‘Apple Care on Device’, and Apple School Manager were facing outages.

Many users online also reported being signed out of services and unable to sign back in. Others reported being unable to activate new iPhones.

Apple has not publicly commented on the development so far. However, the company told Bloomberg the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. 

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement reportedly read.

This follows a string of major outages at big tech giants. On November 12, Microsoft Outlook and Teams went offline worldwide for more than 30 hours after several of Microsoft’s servers became unexpectedly unavailable, placing additional pressure on the remaining infrastructure.

Prior to this in April, AI giant OpenAI also faced a partial outage which has impacted operations of its chatbot, ChatGPT, and agentic coding platform Codex and API platform. In March too, the Sam Altman-led company was also hit by an outage that left ChatGPT unavailable for thousands of users.

The outages have renewed concerns over enterprise dependence on a handful of providers, with experts flagging the need for stronger business continuity plans and multi-vendor redundancy.

Given the recent surge in AI-driven cyberattacks, social media users continue to speculate the reason behind the outages. So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.

item.title: Olyv Raises $6 Mn To Expand Financial Services Play Beyond Lending
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Despite advances in financial inclusion, a large section of India’s salaried and self-employed population continues to struggle to access formal…
item.content:encoded:
Despite advances in financial inclusion, a large section of India’s salaried and self-employed population continues to struggle to access formal credit. The challenge is particularly pronounced in smaller towns, where borrowers often lack conventional income documentation or established credit histories.

Fintech startup Olyv is looking to bridge this gap by expanding beyond digital personal loans into a broader financial services ecosystem focused on credit access and financial health.

Founded in 2016 by Rohit Garg, Amit Chandel, Vinay Singh and Jayant Upadhyay, the startup has raised $6 Mn (around ₹57 Cr) from Nippon Life India AIF Management Ltd and existing investors. The latest fundraise takes its total equity capital raised to around $50 Mn. Olyv has also raised $150 Mn in debt funding since inception.

The latest investment is an extension of its $23 Mn Series B round in February, led by Nandan Nilekani-backed Fundamentum Partnership.

In a conversation with Inc42, CEO and cofounder Garg said the fresh capital will primarily go towards investments in AI and data science to strengthen the company’s proprietary underwriting technology. These investments are aimed at improving risk assessment and personalising financial products, particularly for customers outside India’s major metropolitan markets.

Olyv also wants to deepen its engagement with existing customers by introducing products beyond personal loans. In the near term, it plans to expand into health insurance and credit health management.

The startup is also developing AI-powered financial advisory services to help customers understand their financial data, improve their credit scores and make better financial decisions.

“The idea is that there should be a personalised companion which can help people build their credit scores and manage their data. AI advisory will help them look at their data deeply, advise them and guide them towards actions to create a much stronger credit profile,” Garg said.

Olyv’s $1 Bn Ambition

Olyv operates in a competitive digital lending market, where fintechs such as Navi, KreditBee and Fibe are vying for a larger share of India’s consumer credit market.

However, Garg believes the market is expanding fast enough to accommodate multiple players, with digitisation and financial inclusion bringing more consumers into the formal financial system.

“While the top 50-100 Mn consumers in India are adequately served by large institutions, the next 200-300 Mn is where I believe the next phase of growth over the next decade will come from, and I think Olyv will play a significant role in that,” he said.

The startup claims that 70-75% of its customers come from Tier II, III and IV towns. These include micro-merchants running small neighbourhood businesses, freelancers and salaried employees working with smaller organisations.

Olyv currently has nearly 2 Mn monthly active users and more than 50 Mn app downloads, with a presence across over 19,000 pin codes. It has disbursed approximately 80 Lakh loans, facilitating cumulative transactions worth more than ₹13,000 Cr.

According to Garg, the company currently manages assets under management (AUM) of nearly ₹2,000 Cr. It is targeting 100 Mn users and AUM of more than $1 Bn (around ₹9,348 Cr) by FY29.

While Garg declined to disclose the company’s absolute financials, he said revenue grew around 50% year-on-year (YoY) in FY26, while profit after tax (PAT) increased 80-90%. Olyv also claims to have recorded sequential PAT growth for 14 consecutive quarters.

Inc42 Take: Can Olyv Become More Than A Lender?

Olyv has built a sizable digital lending business by targeting consumers who often remain underserved by traditional financial institutions. Its reported profitability and loan disbursement numbers suggest that it has established a meaningful presence in this segment.

However, expanding from lending into a diversified financial services business is a considerably bigger challenge. Offering health insurance, credit management and AI-led financial advisory services will require capabilities beyond underwriting and loan distribution.

The immediate test will be whether Olyv can convert its existing customer base into users of these additional services. A large lending customer base offers a distribution advantage, but it does not automatically translate into demand for insurance or financial advisory products.

The startup will also need to demonstrate that these new verticals can generate meaningful revenue without disproportionately increasing customer acquisition and operating costs.

There is also the question of asset quality. As Olyv expands its lending business among customers with limited formal credit histories, maintaining underwriting discipline will be critical. Investments in AI and data science could strengthen its risk assessment capabilities, but the effectiveness of these systems will ultimately be reflected in loan performance.

Olyv’s ambition to reach 100 Mn users and cross $1 Bn in AUM by FY29 is therefore not just a question of scaling its existing lending business. It will need to show that it can build commercially viable financial services around that lending base while maintaining profitability and asset quality.

item.title: Perplexity May Launch IPO As Early As Q1 CY27: CEO Aravind Srinivas
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: AI major Perplexity has preponed its proposed IPO timeline and could file its draft IPO papers for a listing in…
item.content:encoded:
AI major Perplexity has preponed its proposed IPO timeline and could file its draft IPO papers for a listing in the US as early as Q1 2027.  

Speaking with CNBC, founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas revealed that Perplexity has managed to grow faster than expected which pushed the decision to fast-track the listing.

“The rate at which our business is growing, I wouldn’t rule out filing something in the first quarter of 2027,” Srinivas said during the broadcast. 

As per him, the company has already touched an ARR (annual recurring revenue) of $1 Bn, surpassing its $750 Mn ARR expectations ahead of the IPO. This allows the company to move the IPO timeline from the erstwhile target of 2028. 

Earlier in 2025, Srinivas had said that the company will not go public prior to 2028 regardless of how the IPOs of AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic perform. Both of the aforementioned AI giants are in the process of listing in the US. 

In fact, Anthropic is set to list on the US Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday. The $64 Bn IPO, which values the Claude parent at $1.4 Tn, valued each share at $70-78. Meanwhile, OpenAI filed for an IPO confidentially back in June and is eyeing a public listing by next year. 

Perplexity AI was founded in 2022 by Srinivas, Denis Yarats, Johnny Ho, and Andy Konwinski, about seven years after OpenAI. The company offers an AI answer and research engine which has been downloaded over 80 Mn times. 

Its largest market is India, as per the founder. To achieve traction in India, the company partnered with Airtel last year. The deal saw Airtel bundling a free one-year subscription of Perplexity Pro to its entire user base of 360 Mn. This led to an immediate 625% month-on-month increase in downloads to 5.9 Mn in July 2025, which later peaked at 22 Mn in October 2025. 

Notably, Perplexity’s app downloads in India declined to nearly 14 Mn by July 2026 after the promotional offer ended. However, its estimated monthly revenue from India rose from $34,000 in January 2025 to $156,000 in July 2026, according to TechCrunch. 

More recently in June this year, Perplexity partnered with Tech Mahindra. The IT services major deploys Perplexity Enterprise Pro across its sales and customer-facing teams, including customer partners and senior sales leaders.

item.title: FirstCry Retains FY27 Growth Guidance, Expects Stronger Q3
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: Omnichannel kidswear and baby products company FirstCry expects revenue growth to pick up in the December quarter (Q3 FY27) on…
item.content:encoded:
Omnichannel kidswear and baby products company FirstCry expects revenue growth to pick up in the December quarter (Q3 FY27) on the back of festive demand. The company also expects gross margins to improve as discounting in the diaper category eases. 

Speaking during the post-results earnings call yesterday, management retained its mid-teen revenue growth guidance for FY27 and said it expects revenue from its India multichannel business to grow in the mid to high teens.

The outlook follows a September quarter in which FirstCry’s consolidated net loss narrowed 75.1% YoY to ₹12.6 Cr and operating revenue rose 14.1% to ₹2,395.8 Cr. Revenue from its India multichannel business, which includes its ecommerce platform and physical stores, rose 18.6% to ₹1,637.9 Cr, its fastest growth in eight quarters.

FirstCry attributed the India business’ growth to investments in its own delivery network, an expansion of its quick commerce service, and changes to the products it stocks in stores.

Its RocketBees network now handles more than 60% of online shipments, while FirstCry Qwik offers deliveries within one to three hours across 16 cities. The company said online purchase frequency rose more than 10% among customer cohorts in cities served by RocketBees.

Diaper Discounting Eases

FirstCry’s consolidated gross margin fell to 35.1% in Q2 FY27 from 36.7% a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA declined to ₹117.5 Cr from ₹120.8 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA margin narrowed to 4.9% from 5.8%.

Management attributed the margin pressure to heavy discounting in the diaper category, higher crude-linked raw material costs, and a delay in passing those costs on to customers. It said competition in diapers started easing in Q2 and cited early signs of a gross margin recovery in October. It expects manufacturing margins to recover from Q4 FY27 if input prices stabilise and the company passes on earlier cost increases to customers.

Meanwhile, revenue from FirstCry’s international operations rose 5.8% YoY and its adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed 15.9%. GlobalBees recorded 7.7% revenue growth and an 83.5% rise in adjusted EBITDA. FirstCry said a warehouse transition at one of GlobalBees’ core brands weighed on revenue growth during the quarter and has since been completed.

FirstCry’s annual unique transacting customer count rose 10% YoY to 12.1 Mn, while consolidated GMV increased 9.2% to ₹3,077.5 Cr in Q2.

FirstCry Shares Rise Over 13%

Shares of Brainbees Solutions, which operates FirstCry, closed 13.3% higher at ₹179.30 on the BSE today. The stock touched a 52-week low of ₹156.55 during the session. At the close, the company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹9,361.1 Cr, slightly over $1 Bn. The shares remain nearly 71% below their BSE listing price of ₹625.

JM Financial retained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock but cut its price target by ₹10 to ₹245, implying an upside of 36.6% from today’s BSE close. The brokerage raised its FY27-FY29 revenue estimates by 1-2% but cut its FY27 adjusted EBITDA estimate by about 18% after Q2 gross margins came in below its expectations. 


It retained its adjusted EBITDA estimates for FY28 and FY29, citing an expected recovery from Q3 FY27 as diaper discounting eases, crude-linked input cost pressures recede, and price increases catch up with earlier cost increases.

item.title: D2C Brand Lumov Eyes ₹33 Cr In Peak XV Surge-Led Round
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: Bengaluru-based D2C orthopaedic products brand Lumov is in talks to raise around ₹33 Cr (about $3.5 Mn) in a funding…
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based D2C orthopaedic products brand Lumov is in talks to raise around ₹33 Cr (about $3.5 Mn) in a funding round led by Peak XV’s Surge programme, sources told Inc42.

The startup’s existing investors are also expected to participate in the round, the sources said.

Lumov and Peak XV didn’t respond to Inc42’s queries on the development till the time of publication.

Founded in 2024 by Saumaric Dangwal and Ankit Gupta, Lumov designs and manufactures orthopaedic braces and other aids for post-surgical recovery, rehabilitation, and pain management.

Both founders have backgrounds in private equity. Dangwal previously worked with Bain Capital as a healthcare and consumer investor, while Gupta was associated with Brookfield Private Equity and Steinberg Asset Management. 

Inside Lumov’s Product Range

The startup’s offerings include knee braces, insoles, and lower-back support belts. The brand sells through its own website, and its products are also listed on Flipkart and Blinkit.

Lumov claims it develops products with orthopaedic specialists at Manipal Hospitals, Apollo Hospitals, Sakra World Hospital, and AIG Hospitals and designs them for Indian patients and local weather conditions.

Prior to this, Lumov raised $1.2 Mn (around ₹10 Cr) in a seed round led by Incubate Fund Asia. QRG Investments and Holdings, the Havells family office, also participated, along with IIMA Ventures, SIDBI, and angel investors including Ashish Gupta of Helion Advisors, Saket Narang of Steinberg India, and Abhishek Goyal of Tracxn.

At the time, Lumov said it would use the capital to strengthen manufacturing, scale sales operations, and develop more products for post-surgical recovery and rehabilitation. It also planned to expand its presence in Delhi NCR, Hyderabad, and Mumbai and deepen its clinical and sales partnerships.

Lumov’s proposed fundraise comes on the heels of another deal in musculoskeletal care products. In September, Bengaluru-based preventive pain care brand Betterhood raised ₹11.5 Cr in a seed round led by Sauce VC.

Investors are also backing startups that provide pain management and rehabilitation services. In January, chronic pain clinic chain Nivaan Care raised $7 Mn in a Series A round led by Sorin Investments. Musculoskeletal care startup Stance Health, which offers physiotherapy and rehabilitation, raised $1 Mn in pre-seed funding in April 2025.

item.title: Claude Outpaces ChatGPT, Gemini In India Adoption
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Anthropic’s AI bot Claude is close on the heels of Indian AI market leader ChatGPT, with the former’s adoption outpacing…
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s AI bot Claude is close on the heels of Indian AI market leader ChatGPT, with the former’s adoption outpacing OpenAI’s offerings significantly over the past few months. Downloads for Claude in India jumped 15X in the September quarter compared to the same period last year, as per data released by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. 

Meanwhile, downloads of ChatGPT declined by 21% over the same timeframe. However, the app maintained its position as India’s market leader among GenAI apps. 

In terms of consumer spending on in-app purchases, ChatGPT continues to sit in the second position only behind Google’s Google One. Its India revenue has also increased by 70% since Q2 FY26 despite increasing its downloads at a slower rate. 

Google One is not just an AI subscription service but also bundles cloud storage in the cost of the plan, which makes a direct comparison difficult. 

Meanwhile, Claude leveraged its growth to climb to third rank from fifth a year ago, overtaking major consumer platforms such as Instagram and YouTube, as its in-app purchase revenue surged in line with its downloads. 

Interestingly, Google’s Gemini AI app reported a 44% YoY rise in revenue in Q2 FY27 despite experiencing a 29% drop in downloads. 

On a sequential basis, Claude’s in-app purchase revenue grew 75% from the June quarter while ChatGPT recorded 61% revenue growth. Gemini’s revenue slipped 31% QoQ. 

As Sensor Tower’s data only tracks payments made on Google’s Play Store and Apple’s App Store, the data doesn’t account for revenue generated from direct web-based subscription purchases. However, the numbers indicate consumers’ shifting preferences for AI as the highly competitive market continues to evolve. 

While Claude doesn’t have any localised pricing in India, ChatGPT has an exclusive plan available in the country called ChatGPT Go, available for ₹399 per month – significantly lower than its Plus or Pro subscription tiers. 

India is ChatGPT’s largest market globally in terms of weekly active users as the platform has doubled its user base in the country since January, OpenAI India MD Prabhjeet Singh said last week. While the company hasn’t disclosed any up-to-date active user count, it had said in February 2026 that ChatGPT had over 100 Mn weekly active users in India. 

Besides, OpenAI has had an office in Delhi NCR since last year and is planning to open additional offices in Mumbai and Bengaluru. On the other hand, Anthropic inaugurated its first India-based office in Bengaluru earlier this year. 

India presents a massive growth opportunity for AI players. As per Inc42’s Bharat AI Startups Report, 2026, the country’s AI market is projected to multiply 5.3X by 2030 to hit $126 Bn and add $1.7 Tn to the GDP by 2035.

item.title: Rediff Files Updated IPO Papers For ₹600 Cr Fresh Issue-Only IPO
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: AvenuesAI subsidiary Rediff has filed its updated draft IPO papers with the SEBI about two months after the regulator cleared…
item.content:encoded:
AvenuesAI subsidiary Rediff has filed its updated draft IPO papers with the SEBI about two months after the regulator cleared its confidential filing.

With the IPO, Rediff, which is one of India’s earliest internet portals and digital media companies, intends to raise ₹600 Cr via a fresh issue of shares. The company had confidentially filed its IPO papers in April 2026, with an estimated issue size of ₹600-800 Cr. 

A large part of the capital raised via the IPO will go towards expanding three businesses — enterprise solutions platform Rediff One; digital payments offering Rediff Pay; video platform Rediff TV.

Rediff has earmarked ₹224.8 Cr for capital expenditure across the three businesses — ₹94.5 Cr on Rediff One, ₹64.3 Cr on Rediff Pay and ₹66 Cr on Rediff TV.

Another ₹183.34 Cr will be used to fuel marketing and branding while the remaining proceeds will be used for acquisitions and general corporate purposes.

Breaking Down Rediff’s Operations

For context, Ajit Balakrishnan founded the company in 1996 with a host of digital services like email services, shopping, news, etc, Rediff has evolved significantly into a tech-led business under the AvenuesAI umbrella. Balakrishnan retired in 2024 after Infibeam (now AvenuesAI) acquired a majority stake in the company. Infibeam’s chairman Vishal Mehta took over as Rediff’s MD in October 2024.

As of now, the company operates across two broader segments: Consumer Digital Platforms (B2C) and Enterprise Digital Platforms (B2B).

Breaking this down further, Rediff operates four primary services in the B2C arena. Its flagship email platform, Rediffmail has 152.46 Mn cumulative registered users as of September 30, 2026. This includes all accounts created since the service was launched in 1998. 

In digital media, Rediff operates Rediff News and Rediff TV, alongside its homepage. The platforms offer current affairs, business information, editorial and video content. Together, they had 90.83 Mn annual active users (AAUs), with an average visit duration of 321 seconds, as of September 2026. Rediff TV, launched in July 2025, is still in the early stages of its business cycle.

The company also operates MoneyWiz, its personal finance information platform, which provides financial news and market data. It had approximately 7.89 Mn AAUs at the end of the September quarter.

Its newest consumer offering is Rediff Pay, facilitates bill payments, P2P transfers, merchant payments through QR codes, and mobile and DTH recharges. Having initially been available to a closed user group, Rediff Pay has transitioned to its full-service phase post NPCI’s TPAP approval. 

On the B2B side, Rediff offers its products under the Rediff One brand. The suite includes Rediffmail Enterprise for business email, rCloud for cloud storage, and Rediff Bol for enterprise messaging. It also operates Rediff Commerce, an ecommerce enablement platform acquired through a business transfer agreement from AvenuesAI. 

The platform helps small and mid-sized businesses build and manage online marketplaces, offering tools for storefront creation, catalogue management, payment integration, inventory, logistics and analytics. It also incorporates AI-assisted features for product categorisation and catalogue optimisation.

Rediff plans to expand these offerings using IPO proceeds. Its proposed initiatives include integrating enterprise resource planning (ERP), customer relationship management (CRM) and human resource management system (HRMS) modules into Rediff One, expanding Rediff Pay’s payments stack, developing Rediff TV into a broader streaming platform and increasing marketing investments.

Rediff’s Financial Snapshot

Rediff reported a net profit of ₹35.2 Cr in the first quarter of FY27 on a top line of ₹58.4 Cr. For the June 2026 quarter, EBITDA (excluding other income) stood at ₹39.43 Cr, translating into a margin of 67.54%.

For the full fiscal year FY26, the company’s operating revenue rose 258.7% to ₹133.6 Cr from ₹37.2 Cr in FY25. Its net profit surged almost 9X YoY to ₹55.9 Cr from ₹5.9 Cr in the previous fiscal year.

EBITDA, excluding other income, stood at ₹65.24 Cr in FY26, compared with a loss of ₹4.29 Cr in FY25. Its EBITDA margin improved to 48.83% from a negative 11.53% over the same period.

The company’s net debt stood at ₹261.48 Cr as of March 31, 2026, rising to ₹354.95 Cr by June 30, 2026. 

Meanwhile, operating cash flow turned positive at ₹160.5 Cr in FY26, compared with an outflow of ₹61.29 Cr in FY25.

item.title: Urban Company To Use ₹600 Cr From QIP To Expand InstaHelp In ₹12,000 Cr Market
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Opening its ₹2,500 Cr qualified institutional placement (QIP) for subscription today, Urban Company has outlined a ₹600 Cr investment plan…
item.content:encoded:
Opening its ₹2,500 Cr qualified institutional placement (QIP) for subscription today, Urban Company has outlined a ₹600 Cr investment plan to strengthen its 10-minute house help service, InstaHelp. 

The funds will be deployed in the quick household service arm in tranches over the next three years, majorly to fuel service professional minimum guarantee payments, service professional referral payouts, training and onboarding spends. 

The company expects to deploy ₹150 Cr in InstaHelp through FY27, ₹300 Cr in FY28, and ₹150 Cr in FY29.

Rest of the QIP amount is set to be deployed as follows: 

  • ₹540 Cr for marketing 
  • ₹200 Cr for technology development and cloud infrastructure 
  • ₹85 Cr for office rent
  • ₹50 Cr for R&D for its Native products.

“Unorganised providers served approximately 90% of home-services spend in Fiscal Year 2026, organised offline players approximately 9% and online full-stack platforms approximately 0.9%. The online home-services industry is projected to grow at a CAGR of 19-25% to ₹12,000-15,000 Cr ($1.3-1.7 Bn) by Fiscal Year 2031,” the filing added.

On the InstaHelp investment plans, the company outlined several risk factors on pouring in more cash in the bleed-heavy segment, where it locks horns with emerging players like Pronto and Snabbit. 

The segment recorded an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹174 Cr in the second quarter of FY27, up from ₹132 Cr in the preceding quarter. This is despite InstaHelp delivering over 1 Cr orders in the first half of the ongoing fiscal, generating about ₹124 Cr in net transaction value and just ₹31.8 Cr in revenue.

Excluding InstaHelp, Urban Company’s adjusted EBITDA was ₹97.07 Cr in H1 FY27, while InstaHelp alone lost ₹305.96 Cr, up from ₹54.13 Cr a year ago. This is already above its ₹234.76 Cr loss for all of FY26. 

That puts InstaHelp’s loss at roughly three times the profit earned by everything else, leaving the company with a consolidated adjusted EBITDA loss of about ₹209 Cr for the half. 

Its average order value has gone down to ₹123 in the first half of FY27 from ₹165 in H1 FY26, highlighting reduction in the amount customers are paying per order. The company highlighted two major reasons— lower introductory prices and competitive intensity. 

In a gist, here are the key challenges Urban Company faces in scaling InstaHelp –

Sustained losses: The consumer services giant expects InstaHelp to remain loss-making for some time as it continues to spend on acquiring service professionals, training, technology and marketing. It has also cautioned that there is no assurance of profitability within a specific timeframe.

Uncertain path to profitability: The combination of high investments, operational challenges, competition and regulatory risks could affect InstaHelp’s ability to scale and achieve profitability. Thus, expected returns from the company’s investment in the segment.

Scaling service supply: The company needs to build a large pool of service professionals and train them adequately to maintain consistent service quality. Amid this, supply may not scale at pace with consumer demand.

Limited differentiation: InstaHelp offers relatively generic house-help services, which can also be provided by online and offline competitors. The market it is trying to crack has long been dominated by unorganised players. The segment has limited barriers to entry, making it difficult for the company to differentiate its offering in the short term.

Safety and conduct risks: Service professionals enter consumers’ homes daily, exposing the business to risks such as theft, property damage and inappropriate conduct. If any of such incidents occurs, Urban Company stands to lose out on brand marketability apart from litigation or regulatory scrutiny.

Regulatory uncertainty: The Code on Social Security, 2020 and other regulations governing gig and platform workers, including state-level laws, could increase compliance costs or force Urban Company to change InstaHelp’s business model. 

InstaHelp is directly competing with quick household help startups Snabbit and Pronto, who are also bidding to establish their names in the rapidly expanding market. 

Snabbit claims to fulfill over 35,000 daily orders and crossed 4 Mn home-help jobs during Q1 FY27. However, its  FY26 financials underline the steep cost of building an instant home-services business. The startup reported operating revenue of ₹12.2 Cr, against total expenses of ₹194.8 Cr, translating into a net loss of ₹167.8 Cr. 

On the other hand, Pronto is exploring opportunities in the physical AI space after raising $45 Mn in a Series B funding round in May 2026. At the time, founder Anjali Sardana said the platform was processing 26,000 bookings a day but remained constrained by the availability of trained professionals. 

Meanwhile, Pronto founder Anjali Sardana has also launched Provision Labs, a San Francisco-based venture focused on building data, evaluation and deployment infrastructure for physical AI systems. As part of its effort towards it, Pronto launched Pronto Verified — an opt-in service where domestic workers wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras while performing tasks such as cleaning and dishwashing. 

Overall, the nascent quick home services offerings are gaining size in a $59 Bn home service market in India, as per an IBEF report.

Shares of Urban Company ended today’s trading session 5.80% lower at ₹161.65 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: Sarvam AI Opens Token Factory To Run Global AI Models On Indian Servers
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: AI unicorn Sarvam AI has opened Token Factory to developers and enterprises, giving them access to its own and global…
item.content:encoded:
AI unicorn Sarvam AI has opened Token Factory to developers and enterprises, giving them access to its own and global AI models through a single application programming interface (API). The company runs the models on GPU clusters in India.

Token Factory hosts Sarvam 105B alongside global open-weight models including Google’s Gemma 4 31B, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3, and Kimi K3.1 Pro. Developers can switch between supported models through the OpenAI-compatible API without setting up their own computing infrastructure.

The platform charges customers based on the number of tokens they send to a model and the number it generates in response. Sarvam’s catalogue lists Sarvam 105B at ₹15 per Mn input tokens and ₹60 per Mn output tokens. Cached input tokens cost ₹5 per Mn.

Sarvam claimed Token Factory matches or beats leading global inference providers on speed and cost for most of the models it hosts. In the company’s tests, Sarvam 105B returned its first token in 200 milliseconds and generated 330 tokens per second for a single user.

The company said it serves more than 450 Bn tokens a day on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, with 95.7% of prompt tokens served from cache. The three-tier cache reduces the computation needed when parts of a prompt repeat.

Sarvam first outlined its plans to run its own and global open-weight models on India-based infrastructure at its Sarvam Epoch event earlier this year. It announced general availability for Token Factory earlier this month.

Competition In Local Inference

Krutrim began hosting DeepSeek models on Indian servers in January 2025. OpenAI introduced India-based API inference for eligible GPT-6 Luna workloads on November 12, while Anthropic offers in-country inference for select Claude models through Amazon Bedrock.

In the broader inference market, Sarvam will compete with Together AI and Fireworks AI, which provide managed infrastructure for running open-weight models, and OpenRouter, which gives developers access to hundreds of models through one API. Cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud also offer model hosting and inference services. 

Sarvam’s pitch to enterprises is that they can switch between its own model and several global open-weight models through one API while keeping prompt processing in India. Sarvam says it runs those models on its own GPUs, so requests stay on its infrastructure without being routed to the model developers’ overseas APIs.

For banks and other financial institutions that need to process certain workloads in India, local hosting could help address data residency requirements. Token Factory also offers dedicated GPU capacity, and Sarvam deploys its inference software on premises for critical institutions.

item.title: Instagram Tightens Recommendations For Sexually Suggestive, Violent Content In India
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Meta has tightened Instagram’s recommendation filters in India to show less sexually suggestive and violent content. The changes apply to…
item.content:encoded:
Meta has tightened Instagram’s recommendation filters in India to show less sexually suggestive and violent content. The changes apply to posts from accounts users don’t follow that Instagram recommends across Explore, Reels, and Feed.

In a blog post, Meta said it strengthened Instagram’s default safeguards in India over the past year based on user feedback. Separately, the company has upgraded its detection systems globally with AI models that check posts against Instagram’s recommendation guidelines before surfacing them, without relying on users to report or hide them. 

Meta said users in India now report recommended content about half as often as they did a year ago. The company did not disclose the absolute number of reports or how much content it had filtered out.

Instagram users can further limit sensitive content in Search, Reels, Explore, Feed recommendations, and suggested accounts through Sensitive Content Control. They can also use Political Content Control to see less political content from accounts they don’t follow, or select ‘Not Interested’ from a post or reel’s menu to shape future recommendations.

Meta Faces Regulatory Scrutiny

The recommendation update comes amid regulatory scrutiny of Meta over the alleged circulation and promotion of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. A BBC investigation alleged that paid Instagram ads directed users to Telegram channels offering CSAM.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) summoned Meta executives following the allegations, and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) opened an inquiry.

In September, Meta agreed to report child safety cases directly to Indian authorities through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, operated by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C).

Later, the company said it had taken action against 5.3 Mn pieces of child sexual exploitation content across Facebook and Instagram in India in the first half of 2026. Meta said it identified and acted on more than 98% of that content before users reported it. 

Meanwhile, the Centre is also exploring withdrawing safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the IT Act for social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and X. The protection limits platforms’ liability for user-generated content.

item.title: Ranveer Singh, Aman Gupta Launch Men’s Personal Care Brand H.I.M
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Actor Ranveer Singh and boAt cofounder Aman Gupta have teamed up to launch H.I.M (Handsome Indian Man), a men’s personal…
item.content:encoded:
Actor Ranveer Singh and boAt cofounder Aman Gupta have teamed up to launch H.I.M (Handsome Indian Man), a men’s personal care brand that says its products are formulated for Indian male skin, local climate, and biology.

The brand has debuted with eight products across face, body and hair, priced between ₹299 and ₹899. It claims that each product is powered by IN·XT, a proprietary molecule developed exclusively for H.I.M. The range is available on the brand’s website, Amazon and Blinkit.

The launch seems to be a part of Gupta’s broader plans to build a portfolio of consumer ventures through his venture studio OFF/BEAT, which aims to back new ideas and emerging founders. OFF/BEAT raised ₹100 Cr in a seed funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners in April this year.

According to the brand, men account for nearly half of India’s population but contribute less than a tenth of the country’s beauty and personal care spending. It said products for men have largely been adapted from formulations originally developed for other consumers.

H.I.M aims to address this gap with products designed around Indian male skin and local environmental conditions, including heat, humidity, pollution and hard water.

It said its formulations draw on research into Indian male skin, including an all-male research panel. Its proprietary molecule is designed to improve the penetration of skincare ingredients.

Speaking about the launch, Singh said he realised that existing personal care products were not necessarily formulated for Indian skin, weather and water conditions. He added that he worked with scientists to develop the formulations and tested them from the initial samples through to the final products.

Gupta said Indian men are increasingly becoming conscious of skincare, reading product labels and adopting personal care routines. He cited an 850% increase in searches for men’s skincare routines over the past five years.

H.I.M’s debut range includes a face wash, moisturiser, and sunscreen for face care, an exfoliating body wash, hydrating lotion, and exfoliating soap bar for body care, and a 2-in-1 shampoo and conditioner marketed for hard-water protection and a scalp serum for fuller-looking hair. 

With the launch, the cofounders are looking to tap into India’s growing men’s grooming market. Rising disposable incomes, growing awareness of personal wellness and appearance, and the expansion of ecommerce channels are among the key factors driving the market.

According to IMARC Group, the country’s male grooming products market is estimated to grow from $2.62 Bn in 2026 to $4.46 Bn by 2034.

item.title: Madras HC Bars Blinkit From Using CSK Superfan’s Image Without Permission
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: The Madras High Court has barred Eternal-owned quick commerce platform Blinkit from using the likeness of Chennai Super Kings (CSK)…
item.content:encoded:
The Madras High Court has barred Eternal-owned quick commerce platform Blinkit from using the likeness of Chennai Super Kings (CSK) superfan Saravanan Hari without his written consent.

The interim order came in a suit in which Saravanan has sought ₹1.1 Cr in damages, alleging that a Blinkit newspaper advertisement used his likeness and gave readers the impression that he endorsed the platform. 

Justice P B Balaji observed that the Constitution protects the rights of every individual and that personality rights can extend to people who have built a distinct public identity.

“This is an interesting case, where a diehard fan of the Chennai Super Kings (CSK) has filed the present suit, seeking to protect his individual personality rights,” the court observed.

Inc42 has reached out to Blinkit for comment. This story will be updated on receiving a response.

What Sparked The Dispute?

The dispute stems from a full-page Blinkit ad published in the Chennai edition of The Sunday Times of India on March 23, 2025. The ad promoted a match-ticket voucher offer with the slogan “The men in yellow always deliver”. In the bottom-right corner was a cartoon of a yellow-painted cricket fan with curly hair, a moustache, and “THALA 7” on his torso, giving a double thumbs-up.

According to the plaint, Saravanan developed his match-day look around 2013. It includes yellow face and body paint, lettering across his torso, red lipstick, a curly wig, a thick moustache, dark eyebrows, and his signature double thumbs-up pose.

Saravanan said he has travelled with CSK and attended matches in India and overseas. He cited television appearances, newspaper coverage, brand collaborations, and public engagements, along with his association with CSK, recognition from CSK veteran MS Dhoni, and an appearance in the Tamil film GOAT, as evidence that his look had become recognisable.

Saravanan alleged that the advertisement created a false impression that he endorsed Blinkit. According to him, friends, fans and acquaintances contacted him to ask whether he had formally associated with the company. Some customers dissatisfied with Blinkit’s services even expected him to resolve their complaints, he alleged.

What The Court Ordered

Blink Commerce, which operates Blinkit, said in its reply to Saravanan’s legal notice that the characters in the ad were fictional and bore no connection to him. It also said it would refrain from using the character in future ads as a gesture of goodwill.

Justice Balaji found a prima facie resemblance between the cartoon and Saravanan, pointing to TV and newspaper coverage showing the same pose. The court said the ad could lead readers to believe that Saravanan had appeared in it or consented to the use of his likeness. It granted an interim injunction against Blink Commerce, finding that Saravanan had made out a preliminary case for protection against commercial use of his persona.

Bennett, Coleman & Company Limited, the publisher of The Times of India, denied liability, saying its role was limited to providing ad space and that the advertiser supplied the material. The court said the publisher’s liability would be examined at trial.

The court directed Blink Commerce and the publisher to preserve materials relating to the ad, including artwork, samples, design records, emails, and correspondence with designers and external vendors. It deferred consideration of Saravanan’s separate request to preserve and produce the defendants’ books of accounts until they appear and file their replies.

Besides damages, Saravanan has sought a declaration recognising his distinctive persona as his property and protection against unauthorised commercial use by unknown parties. The matter is listed for December 14.

InstaHelp Weighs On Earnings

Notably, its management has maintained that it can achieve its profitability targets without the fundraise and rejected the suggestion that the fundraise is necessary to offset InstaHelp’s impact on its financials.

item.title: D2C’s ‘Red Label’ Test
item.dc:creator: Meha Agarwal
item.description: Open Amazon, Blinkit or any quick commerce or ecommerce app, pick a bottle of tomato ketchup from a new-age, clean-label…
item.content:encoded:
Open Amazon, Blinkit or any quick commerce or ecommerce app, pick a bottle of tomato ketchup from a new-age, clean-label D2C brand, and take a closer look at the packaging. 

Chances are, you’ll find claims such as ‘no refined sugar’, ‘no artificial preservatives’ or ‘no unnecessary additives’. Now compare it with a conventional ketchup brand, and the ingredient list could tell a different story — added sugar, acidity regulators (INS 260), preservatives (INS 211), stabilisers (INS 415) and thickeners (INS 1422).

For more than a decade, India’s new-age D2C food brands have built their competitive edge around healthier alternatives to everyday packaged foods, with cleaner ingredients and fewer additives.

But this tried-and-tested playbook could soon face its biggest test: retaining their competitive edge when nutritional transparency becomes an industry-wide requirement.

The topic is stirring up quite a storm as India’s food regulator FSSAI wants prominent red hexagonal warnings on packaged foods high in sugar, salt or saturated fats. Unlike nutritional information buried on the back of packaging, these warnings would be displayed prominently on the front. 

The challenge here is that D2C food brands have spent years positioning their products as healthier alternatives. Now, if these products also receive red warning labels for high sugar, salt or fat content, consumers may begin to question their credibility.

However well-intentioned, the proposed changes could force food brands to walk a tightrope between regulatory compliance, product quality and commercial viability. Let’s get into the whats, whys and hows of it all.

A Recipe For Disruption

It was back in 2022 that the FSSAI first proposed a rating system comprising health stars to govern food labels. But so far, there has been no direct action. 

By August 2026, the discussion shifted towards warning labels in red. The food regulator proposed a single-phase rollout in September 2026, under which exceeding the prescribed limit for even one nutrient could trigger a warning. 

However, the proposal remains under judicial scrutiny after the Supreme Court questioned FSSAI’s proposed 365-day voluntary compliance period. FSSAI is yet to notify the final regulations amid industry pushback, noting that it could take approximately four months. 

Currently, some of the most consequential questions raised by industry stakeholders remain unanswered, including whether warnings should be based on added or total sugar, how nutritional thresholds should be calculated, which products should be exempt, and how much time manufacturers should get to comply.

“A lot of it [rules] is still very open to interpretation. Unlikely that brands have started triggering any action … because the scope and impact of the regulation itself is yet not completely clear,” an analyst told Inc42.

Meanwhile, the stakes extend far beyond redoing packaging. Brands could be looking at new recipes, alternative ingredients, repeated taste trials, laboratory testing and shelf-life adjustments. All of this comes at a cost, particularly for smaller brands already balancing premium positioning with price-sensitive consumers.

Then comes the bigger twist. If avoiding a red warning becomes a priority for the entire packaged food industry, FMCG giants could start reformulating their products too. With larger R&D budgets, manufacturing scale and distribution muscle, they may be better placed to absorb the costs, potentially narrowing the gap that D2C challengers have worked so hard to create.

What’s On The Front Of The Pack Matters

For packaged food brands, the front of the pack is prime real estate, dominated by health claims and brand promises, while crucial nutritional details remain buried on the back. Front-of-pack labelling could upend this equation, influencing not just consumer choices but also product formulations, advertising and competition. 

Several countries, including Singapore, Chile and Mexico, have stringent front-of-pack labelling rules, with some extending restrictions to advertising and sales. The UK, however, follows a voluntary approach. The US follows a mandatory disclosure policy. 

Pluckk cofounder and CEO Pratik Gupta opines that India has long overlooked the importance of making nutritional information visible at the point of purchase. “In India, the back of the pack is already detailed, but nobody reads the back in a store aisle. The front, where you actually decide, still has no rules and that is what should change,” he said.

Gupta also highlighted that the company has voluntarily begun moving ingredient information to the front of its juice packaging and is engaging with FSSAI on greater transparency.

For India’s D2C food brands, however, greater visibility could prove a double-edged sword. Prominent warnings may help genuinely differentiated products stand apart, but they could also expose the gap between a brand’s clean-label claims and its actual nutritional composition. 

And while India’s current proposal does not extend to advertising bans or school-sale restrictions, the global experience offers a glimpse of the broader commercial stakes.

Ultimately, the question is not simply what appears on the front of a food packet, but how that information could alter the way brands formulate, market and compete.

The Cost Of Going Clean

For packaged food brands, the proposed rules could demand more than label changes. According to Prithwi Singh, cofounder and CEO of clean-label staples brand Khetika, reformulation would require balancing taste, shelf life and costs, particularly where sugar, salt or fats play a crucial role.

“Manufacturers would have to balance three considerations simultaneously: taste, shelf-life stability and overall cost. Reformulating a product without addressing all three could compromise the consumer experience,” he said.

He estimates packaging costs could rise 10-20% if better materials are needed to preserve shelf life, excluding one-time redesign and printing expenses. R&D, repeated trials and laboratory testing would add to costs, potentially hitting smaller brands harder than established FMCG players.

Much, however, hinges on FSSAI’s final call. 

For instance, regulating total rather than added sugar could significantly increase reformulation requirements, even for brands that avoid refined sugar, industry stakeholders told Inc42. Rules that govern non-caloric sweeteners remain ambiguous. 

However, not every labelling change is expected to entail high costs. Troovy cofounder Mansi Baranwal recalled revising the brand’s packaging language following regulatory guidance on the word ‘healthy’.

“So, we changed from healthy to good. We didn’t have any such implication, and they gave us some time also. It’s not like our inventory got wasted or anything,” she said.

A three-month transition period allowed Troovy to use existing packaging materials, avoiding inventory losses. However, the change concerned a marketing claim rather than product formulation.

Meanwhile, Pluckk’s Gupta believes brands may need to rethink conventional expectations around taste and shelf life.

“The honest answer is that you cannot make a heavily flavoured, long shelf-life product taste the same once you strip out the sugar, salt and fat because those ingredients were carrying the taste and the stability. But that is not where the market is going,” he said. 

Ultimately, smaller D2C brands will have to face the challenge of absorbing higher compliance and development costs without raising the price of their premium products.

Will Clean Labels Lose Their Edge?

Beyond compliance, the proposed rules raise a more fundamental question about how consumers will distinguish between competing products. 

According to retail and food industry experts, if products with different ingredient compositions carry identical red warnings, the labels could obscure differences that brands have spent years communicating. Much would depend on the final thresholds, exemptions and how consumers interpret the warnings. Once the guidelines are finalised, the onus, therefore, will also fall on brands to re-educate consumers.  

Meanwhile, Pluckk’s Gupta sees an opportunity for new-age brands to shape emerging categories, with regulatory compliance potentially influencing product launches, advertising and shelf visibility.

The Troovy founder, however, cautioned that without clearly defined thresholds and adequate transition timelines, brands could face premature public criticism over their products’ nutritional composition, even before they have sufficient clarity on the new requirements.

Ultimately, the real test for D2C brands will extend beyond meeting regulatory standards to helping consumers understand what those standards mean, and why their products remain worth choosing, and paying a premium for.

THE STARTUP SPOTLIGHT | MUBBLE’s FUNCTIONAL NUTRITION FOR DOGS

  • Mubble is building a pet wellness brand focused on clean, functional nutrition for dogs, addressing everyday concerns such as digestion, skin and coat health, and mobility.
  • The startup combines modern nutritional science with Ayurveda-inspired ingredients to develop targeted nutritional blends, formulated in collaboration with canine nutritionists. 
  • Its product portfolio includes digestive, superfood, shiny coat and mobility blends. As India’s pet care market evolves towards preventive health and specialised nutrition, Mubble is betting on functional products and greater transparency in pet nutrition. 

THE ECOMMERCE BUZZ

NPCI’s New UPI Adoption Plan: The UPI operator has launched a three-year scheme to expand the tech’s acceptance among small merchants, particularly in smaller cities. Funded through MDR collections, the initiative will incentivise banks to deploy QR codes and soundboxes and drive transaction volumes.

Sofina To Invest In PlatinumRx: The online pharmacy startup is in talks to raise $32 Mn in a funding round led by Sofina Ventures at a proposed valuation of $150-200 Mn. The fresh capital could strengthen its affordable substitute medicines business.

Smartphone Sales Tank This Diwali: Offline smartphone sales volumes declined 18-20% during the 2026 Diwali period compared to last year, even as sales value remained broadly flat. According to AIMRA, higher device prices, weak upgrade demand and tighter consumer financing weighed on retail volumes.

THE DEEP DIVE

THE OPERATOR QUESTION

How should food brands approach reformulation without compromising taste, shelf life and commercial viability? According to Pluckk’s cofounder and CEO, Pratik Gupta, here are five key things D2C brands should ponder:

  1. Rethink The Taste Benchmark. You cannot expect a heavily flavoured, long-shelf-life product to taste the same once sugar, salt and fat are removed, because these ingredients contribute to both taste and stability. Instead, explore new product formats where the taste is different, not worse, and consumers are willing to embrace that difference.
  2. Explore Emerging Product Categories. Cold-pressed juices, frozen berries, vegetable chips and clean ketchup are examples of products that offer a different experience. We have seen this first-hand with our 100% fruit juices, which are growing month on month.
  3. Build Compliance Into Product Decisions. Most brands build their portfolios around what sells fastest. Going forward, they will also have to consider what they can actually advertise. Product development will increasingly be shaped by regulatory requirements alongside sales velocity.
  4. Adapt To Different Distribution Channels. Quick commerce is easier to navigate because the pack and product information travel together digitally. The harder, slower challenge is cracking general trade at scale, where shelf visibility and communicating product differences become critical.
  5. Use Transparency As An Advantage. Being a clean-label brand gives us the freedom to push cleaner products, ingredients and communication. Our costs are higher today because of contract manufacturing and small-batch runs, but this is a solvable problem that improves with scale.

item.content:encoded:
D2C Brands Caught In Margin Squeeze

Rising crude prices are squeezing India’s D2C brands. Increasing freight and raw material costs have trapped these emerging brands in a sticky place: absorb losses or risk customer churn. Now, as oil prices begin cooling, can D2C brands find their way out of this Catch-22 situation?

Cost Of Uncertainty: For D2C brands, the challenge is not just higher input costs but their unpredictability too. A single delayed shipment can halt production, forcing brands to pay premiums to avoid disruptions. Imported materials make the problem worse as shipping costs can fluctuate sharply. This leaves founders to choose between paying more to avoid delays or waiting for rates to ease. Either way, working capital takes a hit.

F&Bs Face The Heat: Food and beverage makers face higher exposure than non-food D2C brands as they are more exposed to costs related to commodities and transport. Crude-linked packaging – bottles, preforms, caps and labels – is also adding to the pressure. As such, smaller brands have little room to raise prices and may have to resort to other measures.

The Discount Trap: Unlike established FMCG players, D2C brands rely heavily on ads and discounts to acquire and retain users. Raising prices risks losing customers in a market full of alternatives. Many startups are now considering grammage cuts on entry-level packs and sharper reductions in advertising and discounting. As post-festive demand moderates, brands with strong organic repeat buyers and healthy margins will be better placed to absorb inflation.

Crude Relief Awaits: Although Brent crude has recently retreated from late-October highs, immediate margin relief remains elusive. Because suppliers are still clearing high-cost inventory and freight contracts adjust slowly, lower oil prices will likely take five to six months to filter down to startup procurement bills. 

With gross margins expected to stay under pressure well into next year, how will Indian D2C brands tighten their unit economics until input costs finally normalize? Let’s find out…

From The Editor’s Desk

Bharat Semi Bags  $24 Mn

  • The semiconductor startup has raised around ₹215 Cr in its seed round to ramp up product development, expand its engineering teams in India and the US, and accelerate its GTM efforts.
  • Founded in 2021, Bharat Semi is building programmable smart sensors for physical AI systems. The startup, which is yet to commercialise its technology, plans to initially target clients in the consumer electronics and surveillance markets.
  • With the latest infusion, Bharat Semi is eyeing a piece of the global image sensor market, which is projected to become a $49.8 Bn opportunity by 2030. The space is being driven by growing demand for AI-enabled smart sensors.

Smartphones Get Pricey

  • Samsung and Xiaomi have raised the prices of their smartphones by up to ₹4,000 in India. The hikes impacted around 30 Samsung variants, including Galaxy A07 5G and A17 5G. Xiaomi also revised prices across 19 Redmi variants.
  • The price revisions come amid a broader surge in memory chip prices at the behest of sharper demand from AI infrastructure companies and data centres operators. This has tightened supply chains for smartphone OEMs and pushed up procurement costs. 
  • What has also not helped is the subdued consumer demand. As per industry body AIMRA, offline smartphone sales volumes dipped as much as 20% YoY during the four-day festive period between November 6-9. 

More Troubles For eMudhra

  • CERT-In has now flagged new security flaws in eMudhra’s digital signature utility unit, emBridge. The cybersecurity watchdog has flagged that its software could potentially enable unauthorised entities on the same LAN to view files on an impacted device. 
  • The issue assumes significance as several government portals rely on emBridge for DSC-based signing. However, CERT-In classified the flaw as ‘low-severity’, with eMudhra claiming that keys and token PINs were not exposed.
  • This comes a month after researchers flagged that the private keys behind eight of eMudhra’s intermediate certificates were weak and could be cracked within seconds. The IT ministry has set up a special team to probe the incident.

Eternal Rethinks 2030 EV Goal

  • The foodtech giant is reconsidering its goal of switching to a fully electric delivery fleet by 2030. The company’s chief sustainability officer has said that the deadline “doesn’t look feasible” given the company’s rapid expansion and uneven EV availability.
  • Eternal is now working on a revised date that factors in vehicle availability, government policies and the transport needs of its businesses. The revised target will also cover trucks and smaller commercial vehicles used by Hyperpure, not just two-wheelers.
  • The EV transition of online aggregators faces many headwinds, including expensive financing and high upfront costs of EVs, limited charging infrastructure and unclear residual values. Limited control over fleets also makes large-scale electrification harder.

Fractal’s AI Acquisition Play

  • The listed AI analytics company is in discussions with 20-25 startups for potential acquisitions. Fractal said that its preferred deal sizes will range between $50 Mn and $100 Mn across categories like healthcare, agentic AI and AI engineering.
  • With these acquisitions, Fractal aims to gain specialised engineering talent and strengthen its relationships with large cloud computing firms and frontier AI labs. It claims to have sufficient cash to pursue these deals.
  • The acquisition strategy comes as the company recently said that it expects enterprise AI to scale significantly over the next year as foundation models become more capable and cheaper to run.

Jio’s Desi Satcom Pitch

  • Jio Platforms has begun talks with ISRO, spacetech unicorn Skyroot Aerospace and other Indian launch providers to deploy satellites for the telecom giant’s proposed 1,600-satellite low Earth orbit constellation.
  • The company wants to explore domestic launch options first and is also considering SpaceX for deploying the satellites. Jio is evaluating whether local players can carry out the entire programme from satellite design and testing to launch and deployment.
  • This comes as Jio is preparing to launch a handful of satellites during its upcoming test launch in September 2027. Thereafter, it plans to put 400-450 satellites into orbit by 2030 and complete the constellation by 2035.

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

Can Nova Spectral Make Infrared Vision Affordable?

Conventional cameras fail when darkness, smoke or dust obscure the view. Short-wave infrared (SWIR) imaging can overcome these limits, but its high cost keeps it confined to defence and industrial uses. Enter Nova Spectral AI, a startup that wants to make this capability affordable.

An Affordable Sensor Chip: Founded in 2026, Nova Spectral AI is developing low-cost SWIR image sensor chips. The startup makes its chips using lead-free indium arsenide colloidal quantum dots, which are integrated with silicon CMOS technology. Nova Spectral claims that this approach could make sensors up to 100X cheaper than traditional indium gallium arsenide alternatives. 

The In-House Edge: The startup is building the full technology stack in-house, from quantum-dot ink chemistry and film deposition to charge-transport layers and CMOS readout-wafer integration. Its plans to initially focus on defence, drones and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) use cases. 

A Long Way To Go: Nova Spectral remains at the R&D stage, and its cost-reduction claim is yet to be demonstrated commercially. However, it recently raised funds to expand its team and build a field-ready prototype within 18 months. It is now looking to roll out a sensor-chip prototype by 2028, and is eyeing field pilots in 2029. 

With the global SWIR cameras and sensors market projected to cross $620 Mn by 2030, can Nova Spectral make expensive infrared vision a mainstream feature for machines?
