item.title: India & Nine Other Nations Sign Joint Declaration To Safeguard AI Supply Chains
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: India and nine other nations have signed a joint declaration to safeguard supply chains and infrastructure that are central to…
item.content:encoded:
India and nine other nations have signed a joint declaration to safeguard supply chains and infrastructure that are central to the development and deployment of advanced AI systems. 

The agreement, called the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity, was signed on November 15 at the Pax Silica retreat, which was convened by US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg.

Besides India, the declaration was also signed by representatives of the governments of the US, Australia, Israel, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the UAE and the UK.

“The declaration affirms that economic security is fundamental to national security, sets out the participants’ common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin super intelligence (or AI) supply chains, and declares that safeguarding them is a shared endeavor,” read a statement by the US state department.

For context, the US government refers to AI as super intelligence (SI) after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename it.

The declaration has termed the protection of two strategic assets – “critical” AI infrastructure and “sensitive technologies” – as a “shared endeavour” essential to the prosperity and independence of participating countries. 

The document defines sensitive technologies as goods, software, knowledge, components, inputs and means of production used in AI supply chains. The declaration noted that these technologies could provide a military advantage, create undue economic leverage and pose risks if transferred without authorisation or misused.

It also defines “critical infrastructure” as the physical and digital systems that support AI supply chains, including ports, terminals, transport, communications and logistics networks, information technology and digital platforms. The declaration adds that disruption, hostile control or unauthorised exposure of data flowing through these systems could cause significant harm.

In addition, the signatories also agreed that AI resilience would be “best” achieved through diversified and trusted supply chains and by building trusted capabilities among participants. 

The declaration also underscored the importance of coordinated efforts to address AI supply chain disruptions and non-market policies that distort the AI market. It also called for protecting private investment and ensuring a level playing field for innovation and growth.

To aid this, the declaration also proposed the setting up of working groups across five separate spaces:

  • Pro-innovation policy frameworks
  • AI adoption in key sectors
  • Supply chain cooperation across the AI stack
  • Safe harbours and supply chain security hubs
  • AI security and resilience

“We, the undersigned participants,… reaffirming (reaffirm) the importance of cooperation on the enforcement of our respective policies to protect sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure from undue access, influence, or control, as stated in the Pax Silica declaration…,” added the document. 

The San Francisco Declaration is part of the broader US-led Pax Silica initiative. The framework aims to build secure and resilient supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors and AI infrastructure.

For India, the multilateral platform offers an avenue to coordinate with other economies on AI supply chains and critical infrastructure. This comes as India seeks to expand its domestic manufacturing in semiconductors and advanced computing, while reducing reliance on foreign sources for components and equipment.

item.title: Bombay Shaving Company’s Parent Forays Into Wellness With rE, Eyes Gym Launches

item.content:encoded:
Visage Lines Personal Care Pvt Ltd, the parent entity of D2C grooming startup Bombay Shaving Company, has forayed into the wellness category with the launch of a new brand, called rE.

Cofounded by Bombay Shaving Company chief marketing officer (CMO) Varun Gupta, the new brand sells a range of massage guns, scalp massagers, foam rollers and hot and cold packs. Its website went live on November 16.

In addition, rE also noted that it is also building a separate sub-brand called Republic. Under this, it plans to set up a network of gyms and fitness-centric brands to tap into the recovery and health category. 

Meanwhile, rE’s current product portfolio spans 14 stock-keeping units (SKUs), which will target consumers who spend long hours at desks. As per its website, products start from ₹349 for an eye mask and go all the way to ₹9,999 for a foot massager.

“… A reset that takes ten minutes and is designed with doctors, not just around them, can become a habit. We think rE can help make daily recovery as normal as brushing your teeth,” said Bombay Shaving Company founder and CEO Shantanu Deshpande.

In a statement, the startup also said that rE is pursuing partnerships with brands in areas such as fitness, sports and workplace wellness. 

“rE is pursuing partnerships across fitness, sport and workplace wellness, with a focus on bringing recovery into environments where people already train, compete and work. These include recovery zones at marathons and HYROX events, gym recovery corners and office wellness programmes,” added the new brand in a statement.

rE enters a recovery and wellness market where demand is being shaped by rising gym participation, sedentary work patterns and greater consumer spending on self-care. The brand is positioning itself around daily routines, with products intended for use after work, during commutes and before sleep.

Despite its routine-led pitch, the segment remains highly competitive. At the premium end, US-based companies like Therabody and Hyperice have built positions in percussion therapy and recovery technology. Homegrown brands like Cult, AGARO, Dr Physio and Nextup also sell massage guns, foot massagers and allied devices across lower price points.

That said, rE represents Bombay Shaving Company’s expansion beyond grooming. But its work is cut out as the brand will have to establish product credibility, distribution reach and service infrastructure against established brands.

item.content:encoded:
AI-native customer relationship management (CRM) platform Dreamteam, cofounded by former Freshworks executives, has emerged out of stealth mode. The startup has now raised $53 Mn (nearly ₹498 Cr) in a strategic funding round from Together Fund, Accel and Premji Invest.

The startup did not elaborate how it plans to utilise the funds. 

“… CRM is among the biggest software categories ripe for disruption. I’ve worked alongside Dreamteam’s founders since day one as their vision for an AI-native CRM took shape. Their deep CRM expertise and proven record of scaling enterprise software make them uniquely positioned to lead this reinvention,” said Together Fund cofounder and partner Girish Mathrubootham.

Founded in 2025 by former Freshworks executives Anand Venkatraman, Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy, Dreamteam is building an AI-powered CRM platform. Its four AI agents help enterprises track commitments, flag pipeline risks and automate routine sales workflows.

The startup claims that its AI platform pulls data and context from customer conversations, emails and Zoom interactions to enable AI coworkers to automate regular work. In addition, it also allows businesses to create custom apps and dashboards using natural language without writing code.

Dreamtech claims to already cater to hundreds of companies across industries such as AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing, and consulting. 

Going forward, Dreamteam said that it plans to focus on expanding its use cases across the entire customer lifecycle, including prospecting, onboarding and upselling. 

The fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in Indian AI startups. As per Inc42 data, homegrown AI ventures raised $438 Mn across 35 deals in Q2 2026, up 265% YoY. Venture capital (VC) and private equity (PE) firms remain bullish on startups that help enterprises put AI to work across business functions.

Just last month, US-based AI code testing startup Blacksmith bagged $66 Mn in its Series C round led by Sequoia Capital. Prior to this in October itself, another enterprise AI startup AuxoAI also raised $20.7 Mn in its Series A funding round led by NTTVC.

Fractal Analytics CEO Srikanth Velamakanni also recently reportedly said that the AI analytics company is in discussions with 20-25 AI startups for potential acquisitions. 

At the heart of all this is the growing Indian enterprise AI ecosystem, which is projected to become a $71 Bn opportunity by 2030.

item.title: Oil Cools, But D2C Brands See No Way Out Of Price Hikes
item.dc:creator: Gargi Sarkar
item.description: Direct-to-consumer (D2C) startups have been facing mounting cost pressures since the US-Iran conflict drove up global crude prices, making it…
item.content:encoded:
Direct-to-consumer (D2C) startups have been facing mounting cost pressures since the US-Iran conflict drove up global crude prices, making it increasingly difficult for them to protect their already-thin margins.

Even as higher oil prices push up freight, logistics, packaging and raw material costs for new-age brands and manufacturers, revising price tags does not seem to be a viable option for them for their lack of scale and bargaining power, leaving them grappling for alternatives. 

Unlike established fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) companies, which can leverage bulk procurement, supplier bargaining power, and diversified portfolios to absorb cost shocks, smaller D2C brands have far fewer buffers. 

Absorbing the increase depletes their already unsure margins, while passing it on to consumers risks losing them and reacquiring them at a higher cost. It’s a catch-22 situation for them.

The pressure is particularly visible in categories such as food, beverages and personal care, for which crude-linked packaging, agricultural commodities and imported ingredients account for a significant share of procurement costs. 

Higher shipping expenses and volatility in supplier availability have added to the challenge, making it difficult for startups to plan inventory and input requirements.

The festive season did offer some respite on the demand side. Online festive sales grew 17% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹1.41 Lakh Cr in 2026, according to Datum Intelligence’s Festive Barometer. 

Elsewhere, ClickPost’s analysis of more than 80 Mn orders across nearly 400 D2C brands indicated that daily orders increased 27% YoY in the run-up to Diwali, while estimated gross merchandise value (GMV) grew 45%.

The problem is that this has not necessarily translated into an easier operating environment for D2Cs. Brands are struggling now to sustain consumer demand beyond the festive period while managing the cost of acquiring customers, fulfilling orders and replenishing inventory.

However, there’s some reason for optimism now. Brent crude, which surged to around $118 per barrel in late October, has since cooled to approximately $95 as of November 16, offering a possible reprieve to businesses grappling with rising input costs. For D2C brands, however, the relief may take time to materialise, as the impact of lower oil prices will take a while to filter through to supply chains, freight rates and packaging costs.

For D2C startups, the bigger question is no longer whether input costs will ease, but how long they will have to absorb the pressure.

How Brands Are Absorbing Cost Spikes

The bigger challenge for startups is not necessarily the rise in input costs itself, but the unpredictability of procurement prices, which makes cost planning and margin management very difficult, said the founder of a large D2C beauty brand who preferred not to be named. 

“What bothers startups most is the variation. If a supplier does not stock one product because the price has gone up, the full production (line) might stop,” he said.

For instance, a specialised ingredient may become unavailable because a supplier is unwilling to maintain inventory amid an uncertain price environment. Even if it accounts for a relatively small share of the final product’s cost, its absence can disrupt the manufacturing process altogether. “You cannot make any product with 99% ingredients. That one missing ingredient will hold the thing. Then you scramble and get it from somewhere at any cost,” the founder quoted above added. 

Brands that rely on imported ingredients or packaging materials feel the pinch harder. Shipping costs can fluctuate sharply, forcing them to choose between paying a premium to avoid production delays and waiting for freight rates to ease. Either way, higher procurement costs and the need to hold extra inventory strain working capital, leaving less money for scaling-up.

Bharat Birla, executive director at Anand Rathi Investment Banking, said rising commodity and packaging costs have squeezed larger FMCG companies too, particularly in home care, packaged foods and personal care. But for smaller brands, which lack comparable procurement scale, the impact on operating margins can be far more pronounced, he pointed out.

Food & Beverage Startups Face Most Cost Exposure

The impact of input inflation varies depending on the product category. For several non-food D2C businesses, the cost of goods sold (COGS) may account for around 15-20% of the product price, and at most 30%, according to a large D2C beauty brand founder who did not wish to be named. 

Food businesses, on the other hand, can have a significantly higher COGS, sometimes reaching 40%. This makes food and beverage brands relatively more vulnerable to fluctuations in agricultural commodities, packaging and transportation costs.

Crude oil is particularly relevant for beverage manufacturers because several packaging materials, including plastic bottles, preforms, caps and labels, are linked to petrochemical inputs.

Nikhil Doda, cofounder of Lahori Zeera, told Inc42, “Most of our raw materials depend on crude. Our preforms, caps and labels are all affected. That hit was there.” The company did not raise prices specifically to offset the recent inflation, although it implemented selective hikes in April-May 2026 as part of its regular price revision cycle, he added. 

With Reliance’s Campa expanding and Coca-Cola and PepsiCo sharpening their pricing strategies, further hikes could risk weakening its competitive position. “You cannot increase prices when Coke and Pepsi have decreased their prices from ₹20 to ₹10,” Doda said.

So, for emerging consumer brands, the pricing dilemma is sharper: with fewer buffers to absorb cost shocks, they must protect margins without pricing themselves out of the market.

Why Cutting Discounts May Be Easier Than Raising Prices

Unlike established FMCG players with decades of consumer loyalty, D2C brands rely heavily on digital advertising, promotions and discounts to acquire and retain customers, making price hikes risky in a market where consumers have plenty of alternatives. So, mid-sized and smaller companies are having to look at changes in product mix and pack sizes to manage inflation, Birla said.

The room to raise prices, however, is narrowing for all. According to Sandeep Abhange, research analyst – consumer and midcaps at LKP Securities, large FMCG companies have so far absorbed roughly half of the input cost inflation. “HUL faced 8-10% material inflation but took only 2-5% price hikes, while Dabur took 4% against 10% inflation,” he said.

Startups, Abhange said, could increasingly resort to calibrated price increases and changes in pack sizes, particularly at lower price points. Smaller packs may see grammage reductions, while larger packs could see more direct price increases.

Also, brands should evaluate input inflation alongside marketing expenditure, said the beauty brand founder. “For D2C companies, the cost of goods has a relatively limited impact on overall prices in several categories. If some ingredients become twice as expensive, the cost may go up from, say, 18% to 22%, but marketing costs around 30%.”

This means a reduction in marketing expenditure or discounting could sometimes have a greater impact on profitability than a marginal improvement in procurement costs.

Brands with healthy gross margins, repeat customers and efficient marketing strategies may therefore be better positioned to absorb inflation. Those dependent on aggressive discounts and paid customer acquisition could face greater pressure.

The challenge is particularly relevant after the festive season, when promotional activity begins to moderate and brands have to convert seasonal buyers into repeat customers.

Abhange expects another meaningful round of price increases in Q3 and Q4 FY27, particularly across categories such as detergents, soaps, biscuits, noodles and packaged snacks, which remain exposed to crude-linked inputs and agricultural commodities.

Crude Prices Have Cooled, But Will Startups See Relief?

The softening of crude prices has offered some optimism. However, even as expectations of improved global supply have weighed on prices, geopolitical and shipping-related uncertainties continue to pose risks.

For Indian startups, the transmission of lower crude prices into procurement costs is unlikely to be immediate. “Even if crude cools down, the effect on our procurement levels will take at least five to six months. It’s a process, and things should also remain stable,” Doda said. 

Suppliers may still be working with inventory procured at higher prices, while shipping and conversion costs can take additional time to adjust.

Doda added that geopolitical uncertainty makes it difficult to predict when the situation will normalise. If global prices remain stable, he expects the impact to gradually reach procurement costs over the next five to six months. 

Birla too predicts a similar timeline. This means packaging-intensive businesses may have to wait until the first half of calendar 2027 to see a meaningful reduction in some input costs, provided the decline is sustained.

The broader margin outlook, however, remains cautious. Abhange expects gross margins across FMCG companies to remain under pressure through Q3 and Q4 FY27, with stabilisation likely only from Q1 FY28 (April to June 2027) as lower crude prices and easing packaging costs gradually feed through.

The timelines are not necessarily interchangeable for every D2C business. The pace of relief will depend on the category, supplier contracts, inventory cycles and the extent to which a brand relies on crude-linked inputs.

Next Few Quarters Will Test Unit Economics

For D2C startups, the next phase will be about managing growth without allowing higher procurement and marketing expenses to erode profitability.

Lower crude prices offer a positive signal, but the relief will take time to reach procurement costs. For packaging-intensive businesses, the five-to-six-month transmission period cited by Doda and Birla suggests that meaningful cost normalisation may take until the first half of 2027, provided global prices remain stable. 

A broader recovery in FMCG margins could take longer, with Abhange pointing to Q1 FY28 as a possible turning point.

In the interim, D2Cs will have to focus on supplier diversification, inventory planning, reducing avoidable marketing expenditure and improving gross margins rather than relying solely on price increases.

The current cost cycle may not necessarily become a demand-side problem for the sector, but could reveal the difference between brands that have built resilient operating models and those whose growth depends on continuous discounts and external capital.

For emerging consumer businesses, the festive season may have brought more customers through the door, but the bigger test now is whether they can retain those customers, fulfil demand and make money from every additional order.

[Edited by Chinmay Chaudhuri]

item.title: Fractal To Spend Up To ₹1,000 Cr To Acquire AI Startups
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Fractal Analytics is evaluating acquisitions across healthcare, agentic AI and AI engineering as it looks to strengthen its capabilities ahead…
item.content:encoded:
Fractal Analytics is evaluating acquisitions across healthcare, agentic AI and AI engineering as it looks to strengthen its capabilities ahead of an expected scale-up in enterprise AI adoption.

CEO Srikanth Velamakanni told Reuters that the company is in discussions with 20-25 startups for potential acquisitions. The M&A focus would be on gaining specialised engineering talent and strengthening its relationships with large cloud computing firms and frontier AI labs, particularly in areas where Fractal wants to build deeper capabilities.

Velamakanni said the company does not have a fixed acquisition target but is open to deals worth up to ₹1,000 Cr, although there is no minimum deal value. Fractal evaluated around 800 potential acquisition targets over the past 12 months, Reuters reported.

Inc42 has reached out to the company. The story will be updated on receiving a response.

The acquisition strategy is closely tied to Fractal’s expectations of how enterprise AI adoption will evolve over the next few years. During the company’s Q2 FY27 earnings call, Velamakanni said it expects enterprise AI to scale significantly over the next year as foundation models become more capable and cheaper to run.

He pointed to improvements in models’ ability to handle complex problems and longer-horizon tasks, alongside falling inference costs. According to Velamakanni, the cost of what he termed ‘fixed intelligence’ has declined 48% quarter-on-quarter. At that rate, the cost of intelligence from a foundation model could fall 93% over a year.

He expects these changes to make large-scale AI deployment increasingly compelling for enterprises, with the impact becoming meaningful as early as FY28. Velamakanni added that this shift should also reflect in metrics such as Fractal’s revenue per employee.

Against this backdrop, the company is looking at acquisitions that can accelerate its ability to build and deploy complex enterprise AI solutions. Velamakanni said Fractal is evaluating businesses with deep AI engineering talent, strong local presence across geographies and specialised expertise in industrial verticals.

The CEO also stressed that acquisitions would not be treated merely as a growth lever. Instead, they must improve Fractal’s ‘right to win’ by materially increasing its chances of securing future business. The company is looking for deals that can create a multiplier effect on its growth potential, rather than simply adding the acquired business to its existing operations.

Velamakanni said Fractal has a healthy M&A pipeline and that its board is keen to explore the opportunity. He added that the company has sufficient cash to pursue deals and expects to announce more transactions soon.

Earlier in November, Fractal acquired Geneva-based analytics firm PricingOne through its subsidiary Asper for 1.32 Mn Swiss francs ($1.57 Mn). Velamakanni described the transaction as an acqui-hire, which would also give Asper.ai a foothold in Europe.

The acquisition push comes as Fractal sharpens its focus on enterprise AI following an overhaul of its operating model. In April, the company reorganised its business around three pillars: AI-led Transformation, AI Foundations, and AI Work & Workforce.

The structure is intended to strengthen its enterprise AI offerings, build capabilities around agentic AI governance and responsible AI, and help businesses redesign workflows and workforce capabilities for AI adoption. Its agentic AI platform, Cogentiq, is positioned as the common technology layer across the three divisions.

As part of the restructuring, Fractal announced a leadership reshuffle in May, appointing Kunal Jain as head of AI workforce transformation and Suraj Amonkar as chief AI research officer. Matthew Gennone was given additional responsibility as chief commercial officer and CEO of Cogentiq.

Fractal Analytics Q2 FY27

Fractal reported record revenue from operations of ₹956.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, up nearly 20% from ₹798.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Revenue also grew 4.8% sequentially from ₹912.5 Cr in Q1 FY27.

Its net profit more than doubled 139% YoY to ₹79.2 Cr, compared with ₹33.2 Cr in Q2 FY26. However, profit declined sequentially from ₹115.8 Cr in Q1 FY27.

Adjusted EBITDA rose 30% YoY to ₹154.9 Cr during the quarter, while the adjusted EBITDA margin improved 123 basis points to 16.2%. The company attributed the improvement to operating leverage, while noting that investments in AI engineering talent had a short-term impact on gross margins.

Among its business verticals, healthcare and life sciences (HLS) recorded the highest revenue growth of 79% YoY in Q2 FY27. Revenue from banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) grew 30%, while consumer packaged goods and retail (CPGR), its largest vertical, reported 19% growth. Revenue from telecom, media and technology (TMT) clients, however, declined 18% during the quarter.

Fractal attributed its performance to rising revenues, improving margins, increased client spending and growth across key verticals.

Founded in 2000, Fractal provides AI and advanced analytics solutions to enterprises, including Google, Citibank, Nestlé and Wells Fargo. It also earns revenue through licensing and subscriptions for its AI platforms, including Cogentiq, Iqigai and Kalaido.ai.
